question.text: For a Cat I VC fund using DCF on a young, high-growth investee, why does the terminal growth rate assumption dominate the valuation?

answer.text: Because for young companies most of the NPV comes from the terminal value, so changes in g materially shift enterprise value
Because interest rates are very low
Because the explicit forecast period dominates NPV

explanation.text: The Logic: Per PDF Section 11.6: 'The consideration of the terminal growth rate is VERY SIGNIFICANT as it INFLUENCES the value of shares almost all by itself in YOUNG COMPANIES. Since venture capital funds and private equity funds deal with young and growing unlisted companies, the terminal growth rate could be an important parameter for the investor to consider if DCF analysis is being used to measure the value of the company.' The Trap: Interest rates affect WACC not terminal g directly; auditors do not mandate g; for young companies the EXPLICIT period has small/negative FCF so TV actually dominates. The terminal g leverage is maximum for young firms. Cross-Exam Context: XIX-C and CFA L2 both emphasise this. Damodaran's 'dark side of valuation' discusses exactly this sensitivity problem for young firms.
